     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs, unless the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given (see Critical Rules). Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation:
     96	
     97	- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.
     98	- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.
     99	- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:
     100	  1. "Binding layer: `<layer>`." in those words.
     101	  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput".
     102	  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.
     103	  4. "Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.
     104	  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.
     105	- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.
     106	- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.
     107	- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.
     108	
     109	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write "Binding layer: Indeterminate" with the answer to the user's question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.
     110	
     111	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     112	
     113	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     114	
     115	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     116	
     117	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     118	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The answer says "Binding layer:" followed by the layer, and gives the four exceeded checks as minutes at 1 or "no datapoints". A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.
     119	- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.
     120	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     121	- An Indeterminate verdict says "Binding layer: Indeterminate", answers the user's question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.
     122	- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.
     123	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.
     124	- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.
     125	- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.
     126	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     127	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     128	
     129	---
     130	
     131	## Critical Rules
     132	
     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).
     134	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     135	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.
     136	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     137	- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.
     138	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     139	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     140	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     141	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     142	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     143	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.
     144	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     145	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     146	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     147	
     148	## Gotchas
     149	
     150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     151	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     152	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     153	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     154	- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.
     155	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     156	- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.
     157	- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.
     158	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     159	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     160	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     161	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     162	
     163	## Error Handling
     164	
     165	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     166	
     167	## References
     168	
     169	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     170	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     171	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     172	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     173	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     174	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     175	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     176	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     177	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     178	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     179	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "1b4aa6a9-aaf7-4ac3-ac5c-9848e675028f", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_0PLWLoczPEdSFqcgl4nxN8", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Metrics and thresholds by volume type
     2	
     3	Use this file for any judgement about whether a volume or an instance is at a limit. Read the provisioned values from the APIs (`DescribeVolumes`, `DescribeInstanceTypes`). The numbers below are the documented service limits, not targets. Throughput is always in MiB/s.
     4	
     5	## Which dimension binds, by volume type
     6	
     7	| Type | Included or baseline | Maximum per volume | Ratio rules | Burst model | How to judge |
     8	|---|---|---|---|---|---|

     18	## Metric rules that change the verdict
     19	
     20	- `VolumeThroughputPercentage` exists only for Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes. It reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered, not MiB/s. Never use it as a throughput signal on io1 or io2. A healthy io2 volume can read 100% while its MiB/s is low.
     21	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. For io1 and io2, compute the throughput limit from the provisioned IOPS with the rules in the table.
     22	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 to get MiB/s.
     23	- `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` also use the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, which is not the same as 0.
     24	- `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with the `InstanceId` dimension, on Nitro instances that are not bare metal.
     25	- `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only.
     26	- `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds. Average latency in ms per operation = Sum(time) / Sum(ops) x 1,000.
     27	- A 1-minute average hides sub-minute peaks. If the minute average is below a limit but latency and queue length rise, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` at 1 show a burst within the minute; the detailed performance statistics in troubleshoot-performance.md show it at up to 1-second granularity.

     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history with `DescribeAlarmHistory` for the last 24 hours: when it first entered ALARM, and any earlier ALARM and OK transitions. Report earlier transitions as history, because they show whether the pattern recurs.
     17	- Describe the impact in the symptom: the alarm name, metric, threshold, the datapoints that breached it, whether the alarm has actions configured, and the onset (the minute the metric left its normal level, for example "queue length rose from about 0 at `<time>` to 1.5 from `<time>`").
     18	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     19	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     20	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     21	
     22	### Step 2: Build the context
     23	
     24	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     25	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     26	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     27	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     28	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     29	
     30	### Step 2a: Read the exceeded checks
     31	
     32	Read these four CloudWatch metrics early, for the alarm window, at a 1-minute period, with the `Maximum` statistic. They are the most direct evidence of which limit binds.
     33	
     34	| Metric | Namespace and dimensions | A value of 1 means |
     35	|---|---|---|
     36	| `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` | AWS/EBS, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more IOPS than the volume's provisioned IOPS in that minute |
     37	| `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` | AWS/EBS, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more throughput than the volume's provisioned throughput in that minute |
     38	| `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` | AWS/EC2, `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more IOPS than the instance's maximum EBS IOPS in that minute |
     39	| `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` | AWS/EC2, `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more throughput than the instance's maximum EBS throughput in that minute |
     40	
     41	- Read the two volume checks for every attached volume, and the two instance checks for the instance. They exist only on Nitro instances (the instance checks not on bare metal), are not published for Multi-Attach volumes (volume checks), and are not available in AWS Outposts, Local Zones or Wavelength Zones.
     42	- Report, for each check, the number of minutes at 1 and the window, for example "`VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` 1 in 37 of 37 minutes, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC".
     43	- A volume check at 1 is direct evidence that the volume limit binds. An instance check at 1 is direct evidence that the instance limit binds; when both are at 1, the instance is fixed first (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)).
     44	- If a query returns no datapoints, query again with both dimensions. If it is still empty, write "no datapoints", not 0, list it under Gaps, and judge the limit from the measured IOPS and MiB/s in Steps 3 and 4.
     45	- Confirm the checks against the measured values in Steps 3 and 4. The limits table still shows the numbers.
     46	
     47	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     48	
     49	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     50	
     51	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     52	
     53	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     54	
     55	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     56	
     57	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     58	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     59	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     60	- VolumeQueueLength
     61	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     62	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period. That fits volume saturation, an instance limit and impairment, so use Steps 4 and 5 to tell them apart, and do not call the volume saturated on idle time alone. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     63	
     64	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     65	
     66	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     67	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     68	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     69	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     70	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     71	
     72	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     73	
     74	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     75	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     76	- Use the instance exceeded checks from Step 2a. `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` or `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` at 1 during the window is direct evidence that the instance is the binding layer.
     77	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     78	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     79	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     80	
     81	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     82	
     83	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     84	
     85	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     86	
     87	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     88	2. The `VolumeStalledIOCheck` metric for the volume (dimensions `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, Nitro instances only; 0 passed, 1 failed). A failed check (value 1) means the volume's IO is stalled, which is an AWS-side impairment. Escalate per the rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) and never recommend adding IOPS.
     89	3. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     90	4. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     91	
     92	Name AWS-side impairment only when item 1, 2 or 3 gives a direct signal (an impaired status or failed status check, a failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, or an open AWS Health event). If none of the four explains it, report the Binding layer as Indeterminate, keep the cause open, and present the candidate causes with their supporting observations and checks, as described in the Indeterminate section of [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). Tell the customer to check the AWS Health Dashboard and the volume status checks, give the [detailed performance statistics](#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) step for the customer to run during the symptom, and follow the escalation rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md).
     93	
     94	If the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given, run this step on those values only. Do not query the account for other volumes or alarms.
     95	
     96	Filter the AWS FIS, AWS Health and AWS CloudTrail results to the volume, its instance and the volumes attached to that instance. Report only what applies to them, for example "no running AWS FIS experiment targets this volume or instance". Do not describe experiments, changes or alarms on other resources.

     99	
     100	Run this step for every performance verdict.
     101	
     102	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` for every attached volume. It returns only the most recent modification of each volume, so it shows the latest change and its state, not the full history.
     103	- AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` for `ModifyVolume` on the affected volume over the last 24 hours, and for `AttachVolume`, `DetachVolume` and `ModifyInstanceAttribute` on the instance. Second, the demand trend: demand that grew while latency per I/O stayed flat is growing load reaching a limit; latency per I/O that rose at the same demand points to a slowdown instead.

     123	## Other performance topics
     124	
     125	### Micro-bursting
     126	
     127	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.
     128	
     129	Check the exceeded checks from Step 2a first. The Amazon EBS User Guide says `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` return 1 when the driven IOPS or throughput consistently exceeds the provisioned value for any second within the minute, so they show bursts that the minute averages hide. If the checks are 0 or have no datapoints and the question is still open, give the customer the detailed performance statistics step below.
     130	
     131	### Detailed performance statistics (a step the customer runs)
     132	
     133	Amazon EBS NVMe devices on Nitro instances keep detailed performance statistics that the customer reads on the instance, at up to 1-second granularity, for any volume type, at no extra cost. There is no AWS API for them, so the agent never runs this step. Give it to the customer as a step to run when the 1-minute CloudWatch data cannot settle the question, for example suspected micro-bursting, or an Indeterminate verdict.
     134	
     135	Tell the customer to connect to the instance the volume is attached to, find the volume's NVMe device name (see the device mapping link in Sources), and run one of the documented commands:
     136	
     137	- Linux, `nvme-cli` (included in Amazon Linux AMIs released after November 12, 2024; on older AMIs run `sudo yum install nvme-cli` first): `nvme amzn stats /dev/nvme0n1`
     138	- Linux, the `ebsnvme` script from the amazon-ec2-utils GitHub repository:
     139	  `wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amazonlinux/amazon-ec2-utils/refs/heads/main/ebsnvme`, then `sudo chmod +x ./ebsnvme`, then `sudo ./ebsnvme stats /dev/nvme0n1`
     140	- Windows, AWSNVMe driver version 1.7.0 or later, as Administrator: `.\nvme_amzn.exe stats <disk_number>`
     141	
     142	Replace `/dev/nvme0n1` or `<disk_number>` with the volume's device. The customer can also collect the statistics with the Amazon CloudWatch agent as custom metrics.
     143	
     144	What to look at:
     145	
     146	| Statistic | What it shows |
     147	|---|---|
     148	| `ebs_volume_performance_exceeded_iops`, `ebs_volume_performance_exceeded_tp` | Total time, in microseconds, that demand exceeded the volume's provisioned IOPS or throughput |
     149	| `ec2_instance_ebs_performance_exceeded_iops`, `ec2_instance_ebs_performance_exceeded_tp` | Total time, in microseconds, that the volume exceeded the instance's maximum EBS IOPS or throughput |
     150	| `volume_queue_length` | Read and write operations waiting to complete, at that point in time. Stalled or impaired I/O shows here |
     151	| `read_io_latency_histogram`, `write_io_latency_histogram` | Completed operations per latency bin, in microseconds. Only completed I/O is counted |
     152	| `total_read_ops`, `total_write_ops`, `total_read_bytes`, `total_write_bytes`, `total_read_time`, `total_write_time` | Completed operations, bytes, and time in microseconds |
     153	
     154	The counters add up from the time the volume was attached, so ask for two readings taken a known number of seconds apart during the symptom and compare the difference. Exceeded time that grows between the readings shows the volume or instance limit binds for part of each second, even when the 1-minute averages are below it. No growth in exceeded time, together with a growing queue or a latency histogram that moves to higher bins, supports a slowdown rather than a limit.
     155	
     156	### Volume initialization after restore
     157	
     158	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized. Check `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime`. If the volume was recently restored, explain initialization and point to fast snapshot restore (`DescribeFastSnapshotRestores`) and the initialization guide. This is not a provisioning problem.
     159	
     160	### Burst credits
     161	
     162	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.
     163	- Instance level: some smaller instance sizes publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. Draining or at 0 means the instance has dropped or will drop to its EBS baseline. Recommend an instance type whose baseline covers the measured demand.
     164	
     165	### How much IOPS or throughput to provision
     166	
     167	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     168	2. Apply the type rules (gp3: up to 500 IOPS per GiB and 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS; io2: up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, and throughput up to 0.256 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS; io1: up to 50 IOPS per GiB) from [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md). For io1 and io2, check that the IOPS value also gives the throughput limit the workload needs.
     169	3. Check the instance's remaining EBS baseline: baseline minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     170	4. Propose the smaller of the measured need and what the instance can deliver. If the need exceeds the instance baseline, say so and recommend an instance type change.
     171	5. State how the target was computed.

     33	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.

     5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).
     8	- Size can only increase. It cannot be reduced. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.
     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     12	- After a size increase, the operating system must extend the partition and the file system. The agent gives the commands; the operator runs them.
     13	- Read the requirements page before proposing a change on an older instance, or on a volume with an MBR partition (2 TiB limit).
     14	
     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.
     19	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s at 128 KiB I/O and IOPS at 16 KiB I/O. Convert MB/s to MiB/s before comparing with volume throughput.
     20	- Some smaller instance sizes burst above the baseline for a limited time and publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. When those balances drain or reach 0, the instance drops to its baseline.
     21	
     22	## Quotas
     23	
     24	- Amazon EBS quotas are per Region. Check each Region the user works in.
     25	- Discover quota codes by name with `ListServiceQuotas --service-code ebs`. Never hardcode quota codes.
     26	- Read defaults from the Amazon EBS quotas page. For example, the default for snapshots per Region is 100,000 and it is adjustable.
     27	- The io2 regional IOPS quota is separate from the per-volume maximum. A request within the per-volume maximum can still fail on the regional quota. Existing io2 volumes already consume part of that quota.
     28	- Adjustable quotas are raised through Service Quotas. Quotas that are not adjustable need an AWS Support case.
     29	
     30	## Snapshots
     31	
     32	- Snapshots are incremental. Deleting a snapshot might not reduce storage cost, because later snapshots can reference its blocks. Any savings figure is an upper bound.
     33	- You cannot delete a snapshot that is the root device snapshot of a registered AMI, even if the AMI is deprecated or disabled. Deregister the AMI first, and only if it is no longer needed.
     34	- Snapshots created by AWS Backup are managed in AWS Backup, not with Amazon EC2 delete calls.
     35	- Identify Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager snapshots by `aws:dlm:*` tags, never by the snapshot name or description. A snapshot can be named like a DLM snapshot and still have no `aws:dlm:*` tags.
     36	- Target tags for Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies are case sensitive.
     37	- Recycle Bin rules decide whether a deleted snapshot can be recovered. With no matching rule, deletion is permanent.

     24	## Metric rules
     25	
     26	AWS/EBS publishes 1-minute data.
     27	
     28	| Namespace | Metrics | Dimensions |
     29	|---|---|---|
     30	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeAvgIOPS` (Ops/s), `VolumeAvgThroughput` (KiB/s), `VolumeAvgReadLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeStalledIOCheck` (0 passed, 1 failed), `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` (0 not exceeded, 1 the application tried to drive more than the volume's provisioned IOPS or throughput in that minute; not for Multi-Attach volumes) | `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`. Nitro instances only. A query with `VolumeId` alone returns no datapoints |

     33	
     34	The four exceeded checks and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` are not available in AWS Outposts, Local Zones or Wavelength Zones. They are ordinary CloudWatch metrics read with `GetMetricData`, so they need no extra permission. For the exceeded and stalled checks, report the `Maximum` per minute, the number of minutes at 1 and the time window. "No datapoints" is not the same as 0: say which one you got, and list "no datapoints" under Gaps.
     35	
     36	Metric math from the Amazon CloudWatch metrics page for Amazon EBS. Use `Sum` statistics for ops, bytes and time.
     37	
     38	- IOPS = Sum(`VolumeReadOps` + `VolumeWriteOps`) / period in seconds
     39	- MiB/s = Sum(`VolumeReadBytes` + `VolumeWriteBytes`) / period in seconds / 1,048,576
     40	- Average read latency in milliseconds per operation = Sum(`VolumeTotalReadTime`, in seconds) / Sum(`VolumeReadOps`) x 1,000 (and the write equivalent with `VolumeTotalWriteTime` and `VolumeWriteOps`). Without the x 1,000 the result is in seconds. Always state latency in milliseconds
     41	- Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period in seconds x 100
     42	- MiB/s from `VolumeAvgThroughput` = value in KiB/s / 1,024
     43	
     44	What a 1-minute average hides: sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average looks below it (micro-bursting). When latency or queue length rises while the average sits below the limit, say that headroom is not proven instead of claiming it.
     45	
     46	`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` are published only for some instance sizes (generally 4xlarge and smaller) that can burst. If they are absent, the instance does not publish them. That is not a fault.

## Root cause
The bottleneck is the volume, not the instance. Volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, mounted at /dev/sdf on c6i.xlarge i-1234567890abcdef0_5) has been doing a steady write-only workload since about 18:05 UTC, shortly after the instance launched at 18:05:10. The workload asks for more IOPS than the volume is provisioned for. From 18:10 onward VolumeWriteOps sits at 300,000 per 5 minutes in almost every interval, which is exactly 1,000 IOPS, the provisioned ceiling. Each write is 8 KiB, so throughput is only about 8.2 MB/s and throughput is not the limit. Because the volume is held at its IOPS cap, requests queue up. VolumeQueueLength stays around 1.3–1.5, above the alarm threshold of 1, and the average write time is about 1.5 ms per operation (VolumeTotalWriteTime divided by ops), which is the extra application write latency you're seeing. The instance-level EBS limits are not involved: EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99% the whole time, and total instance EBS IOPS is about 1,500, far below the c6i.xlarge baseline of 6,000. What to change: raise the volume's provisioned IOPS with an online ModifyVolume. io2 allows up to 500 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume can go up to 5,000 IOPS; for more than that, grow the volume too. A reasonable step is 2,000–3,000 IOPS, with enough headroom for the queue to drop below 1. Watch instance bandwidth when you do: the instance is already moving about 140 MB/s of EBS traffic (about 131 MB/s of that is reads on another volume, most likely gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19, which has its own read-bytes alarm). The c6i.xlarge baseline is about 156 MB/s, so adding about 2,000 IOPS of 8 KiB writes (about 16 MB/s) would put it right at that baseline. After the change, watch EBSByteBalance%. If it starts to fall, move to a larger instance (e.g. c6i.2xlarge) or cut the read load on the other volume.
## Evidence
- EC2 DescribeVolumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, Size=10 GiB, Iops=1000, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_5 as /dev/sdf.
- CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength \u003e 1) went into ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:04 UTC.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteOps (5-minute Sum) is 300,000 in nearly every interval from 18:10 to 19:25 UTC (one dip to 272,165 at 19:15) = 1,000 IOPS, exactly the provisioned value. VolumeReadOps is 0.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes is about 2.4576e9 per 5 minutes: 8,192 bytes per op, about 8.2 MB/s, nowhere near io2 throughput limits.
- AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength average is 1.47–1.50 from 18:10 to 19:10 and 1.27–1.33 from 19:15 to 19:30. VolumeTotalWriteTime is about 448 s per 5 minutes, about 1.5 ms average write latency.
- AWS/EC2 EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% for i-1234567890abcdef0_5 hold at 99% from 18:05 to 19:30, so the instance EBS burst budget is not being drawn down.
- AWS/EC2 instance totals: EBSWriteOps about 300.4k plus EBSReadOps about 150.1k per 5 minutes (about 1,500 IOPS, well under the c6i.xlarge baseline of 6,000). EBSReadBytes about 39.3 GB per 5 minutes (about 131 MB/s) plus EBSWriteBytes about 8.2 MB/s, under the roughly 156 MB/s baseline.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_5
- vol-1234567890abcdef0_19
## Gaps
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no data, so the IOPS cap is shown by ops matching the provisioned value exactly, not by that flag.
- I did not look at application or OS-level metrics (in-guest iostat, application latency). The link to the application's write-latency increase is inferred from EBS queue depth and per-op write time.
- I did not break out per-volume metrics for vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 and vol-1234567890abcdef0_16. That the ~131 MB/s of reads come from the gp3 volume is inferred from its VolumeReadBytes alarm.
- I did not check CloudTrail for what started the workload around 18:05, beyond the instance launching at 18:05:10.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

The fast agent also claimed the exceeded checks returned no data, but my own query shows VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 for 87 of 88 minutes between 18:07 and 19:33, directly contradicting that. The instance's LaunchTime of 18:05:10 is interesting given the volumes attached back in November — this suggests a stop/start rather than a fresh launch, and the workload began just two minutes after that restart. Looking at throughput, summed instance MiB/s runs 129–133 against a baseline of ~149 MiB/s, leaving only modest headroom, while one gp3 volume is separately capped at its own 125 MiB/s throughput limit; summed IOPS peaks at 1502.8 against a 6000 baseline. For sizing the recommendation, true demand above 1000 IOPS is unknown since it's capped there, and applying Little's Law to the ~1.5 queue length at 1000 IOPS suggests the application is maintaining roughly 1.5 I/Os in flight.

I'm checking whether this same 1,000 IOPS ceiling has been hit repeatedly throughout the day — alarms fired at 07:43–07:54, 08:02–14:00, 16:23–17:24, and now 18:11 onward, each peaking at exactly 1,000 IOPS (60,002–60,020 ops per minute), confirming a hard, recurring ceiling rather than a one-off spike. Converting the instance's 156.25 MB/s baseline to roughly 149.01 MiB/s and comparing against the current combined usage of about 125.1 MiB/s from the other volumes, that leaves around 23.9 MiB/s of throughput headroom available for the io2 volume, which I'm now converting into an IOPS-equivalent at an 8 KiB I/O size.

I'm working out that roughly 3,000 IOPS sits right at the throughput ceiling the instance baseline allows, staying just under the 149.0 MiB/s limit and well within the io2 volume's own IOPS-per-GiB cap, so that becomes the practical target rather than something smaller like 2,000 — though true demand above 1,000 IOPS can't actually be measured since the volume has been artificially capped the whole time, so I'm leaning on the instance's delivery ceiling as the bounding constraint per the guidance to propose the smaller of measured need and deliverable capacity.

The volume modification history query failed across the board since the root volume had none on record, so I need to rerun it specifically for the io2 volume, plus pull CloudTrail ModifyVolume events for the past 24 hours and check instance events too.

I also want to check what the FIS experiment that kicked off at 19:32:34 actually targets, and I noticed queue length and latency both dropped around 19:16 with a brief dip at 19:15 - worth noting but probably not critical. I'll run describe_volumes_modifications for the io2 volume, fis get_experiment, and CloudTrail lookups for both the volume and instance resource IDs.

The fast agent's claims mostly hold, but two corrections: `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` does return data (value 1), and io2 allows 1,000 IOPS per GiB, not 500. Now checking the running FIS experiment, the volume's latest modification, and CloudTrail history.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### VolumeQueueLength above threshold on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length ([redacted ARN]) moved to ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:04 UTC. The last 3 one-minute averages were 1.50, 1.49 and 1.49, above the 1.0 threshold. The alarm has no actions configured.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:08:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: io2 volume under-provisioned: workload pinned at 1,000 IOPS cap
**Description:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, /dev/sdf on c6i.xlarge i-1234567890abcdef0_5, account 012345678901_1, us-east-1) delivered 999.9–1,000.1 IOPS every minute 18:08–19:33 UTC (single dip to 536 at 19:15), all 8 KiB writes (7.81 MiB/s vs 256 MiB/s throughput limit). VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 in 87 of 88 minutes; throughput and instance-level exceeded checks 0 in 88/88. Little's law fits: 1.5 queue ÷ 1,000 IOPS = 1.5 ms per write, matching measured write latency. The same fixed ceiling (60,002–60,020 write ops/min) bound every busy hour today, and the volume has never been modified.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **Write IOPS pinned at 1,000 provisioned ceiling:** From 18:08 UTC vol-0123456789abcdef0 runs a write-only workload at exactly ~1,000 IOPS (8 KiB I/O, ~7.8 MiB/s), the volume's provisioned IOPS. Queue length ~1.47–1.51 and avg write latency ~1.5 ms/op; dips to ~1.27 queue / 1.27 ms after 19:16 while IOPS stays at 1,000. VolumeIdleTime ~0 until 19:15. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 from 18:07 onward; VolumeThroughputExceededCheck and VolumeStalledIOCheck = 0.
- **Recurring IOPS saturation throughout the day:** Hourly history for vol-0123456789abcdef0 shows the same write workload pinned at ~1,000 IOPS (7.8 MiB/s, ~1.33 ms write latency, queue ~1.33) every hour from 08:00 to 13:00 UTC, with VolumeIOPSExceededCheck set for 60 of 60 minutes in each of those hours. The volume was idle from 14:00 to 15:59, then saturated again at 16:00 (41 min), 17:00 (18 min), 18:00 (53 min) and 19:00 (35 min so far). The queue-length alarm's flapping today follows these workload on/off cycles.
- **Affected volume: io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-a-io2, Scenario a) is an io2 volume with 1,000 provisioned IOPS. It is unencrypted, in us-east-1a, and attached as /dev/sdf to i-1234567890abcdef0_5. The other volumes on this instance are gp3 at 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s: root vol-1234567890abcdef0_20 (8 GiB), vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 (20 GiB, Scenario b) and vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 (200 GiB, Scenario e).

#### Gaps
- **True IOPS demand unmeasurable while capped:** Because the volume is held at 1,000 IOPS, the workload's demand above the cap cannot be measured; the 3,000 IOPS target is sized to instance headroom, not observed demand.

### Hypothesis: Instance EBS limit as bottleneck
**Description:** Four attached volumes summed to at most 1,502.8 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s vs c6i.xlarge baseline 6,000 IOPS / 149.0 MiB/s; EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% min 99%; CPU ~1%; instance exceeded checks 0 in 88/88.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **Instance EBS limits not exceeded:** i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge, Nitro; EBS baseline 6,000 IOPS / 156.25 MB/s, max 40,000 IOPS / 1,250 MB/s): InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck = 0 throughout; EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% minimum 99%; CPU ~1%.
- **Instance EBS traffic is ~133 MiB/s, mostly gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19:** Since 18:08, gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 (example-b-gp3-throughput) has run at ~500 IOPS and ~125 MiB/s, which is its full 125 MiB/s provisioned throughput. vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 is idle and the root volume is negligible. Instance totals are 1,037–1,503 IOPS and 129–133 MiB/s, against the c6i.xlarge baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s. That leaves limited bandwidth headroom for raising IOPS on the io2 volume.

#### Gaps
- **No application or OS-level metrics:** No application or OS metrics were available, and CloudTrail shows nothing that started the workload at 18:07 beyond the instance launch at 18:05:10 UTC.
- **True IOPS demand unmeasurable while capped:** Because the volume is held at 1,000 IOPS, the workload's demand above the cap cannot be measured; the 3,000 IOPS target is sized to instance headroom, not observed demand.

### Hypothesis: Volume impairment or external fault
**Description:** VolumeStalledIOCheck 0 in 88/88 minutes; DescribeVolumeStatus ok / io-performance normal; no open AWS Health EBS/EC2 events; the running FIS experiment targets a different volume (vol-1234567890abcdef0_11).
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **All volumes healthy; alarm has flapped repeatedly today:** describe_volume_status: all 4 attached volumes ok (io-enabled passed, io-performance normal, no events). Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length went OK→ALARM at 07:43, 08:02, 16:23 and 18:11 UTC on 2026-11-23, recovering at 07:54, 14:00 and 17:24.
- **No external cause: Health clean, no changes to the io2 volume, FIS targets a different volume:** AWS Health shows no open EBS/EC2 events, and no modification exists for vol-0123456789abcdef0. In CloudTrail over the last 24h, the only events on i-1234567890abcdef0_5 are read-only AssumeRole calls (18:05:12, 18:47:29 UTC). ModifyVolume was called only on gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 (08:42:58, 16:54:22, 18:52:00 UTC by example-session), never on the alarmed io2 volume. The running FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (started 19:32:35 UTC, aws:ebs:volume-io-latency, 500 ms on 100% of writes and 50% of reads, PT60M) targets a different volume, vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, and started ~80 min after the alarm.

#### Gaps
- **No application or OS-level metrics:** No application or OS metrics were available, and CloudTrail shows nothing that started the workload at 18:07 beyond the instance launch at 18:05:10 UTC.
- **True IOPS demand unmeasurable while capped:** Because the volume is held at 1,000 IOPS, the workload's demand above the cap cannot be measured; the 3,000 IOPS target is sized to instance headroom, not observed demand.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise provisioned IOPS on io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to 3,000 with an online Elastic Volumes change

## Reasoning
The volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS is the only limit being hit (VolumeIOPSExceededCheck 87/88 min; instance checks 0). 3,000 IOPS of 8 KiB writes (~23.4 MiB/s) fits the 23.9 MiB/s left under the c6i.xlarge 149.0 MiB/s EBS baseline. Passed the safe-deployment policy check; not applied — requires operator approval on the approval card. If the volume still hits its cap or EBSByteBalance% drains, the next step is c6i.2xlarge.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Save the current volume configuration as the rollback baseline
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
```
**Purpose:** Save the current volume configuration as the rollback baseline

#### 1.2 Take an optional point-in-time data backup
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-ModifyVolume backup before IOPS 1000->3000" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=snapshot,Tags=[{Key=Purpose,Value=pre-iops-change-backup}]' --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Take an optional point-in-time data backup
**Risks:** Snapshot storage is billed until deleted
**Advisory:** An IOPS-only change does not touch data; rollback uses the saved configuration, not the snapshot

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Confirm no modification is in progress (expect NotFound or completed)
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm no modification is in progress (expect NotFound or completed)

#### 2.2 Confirm volume status is ok; stop if impaired
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volume-status --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm volume status is ok; stop if impaired

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Lift the IOPS ceiling causing write queuing
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Lift the IOPS ceiling causing write queuing
**Risks:** Tripled provisioned io2 IOPS raises cost, Instance left with ~0.5 MiB/s EBS throughput headroom below baseline, True demand is unknown; 3,000 IOPS may still not be enough
**Advisory:** Uses 1 of 4 modifications in a rolling 24 h window

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the change reaches optimizing/completed with TargetIops=3000
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].[ModificationState,TargetIops,Progress]'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the change reaches optimizing/completed with TargetIops=3000

#### 4.2 Confirm the volume reports Iops=3000
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].Iops'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the volume reports Iops=3000

#### 4.3 Confirm the volume IOPS cap is no longer hit
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeIOPSExceededCheck --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_5 --start-time <APPLY_TIME_UTC> --end-time <APPLY_TIME_PLUS_30M_UTC> --period 60 --statistics Maximum --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the volume IOPS cap is no longer hit
**Advisory:** Also check VolumeQueueLength < 1.0, EBSByteBalance% near 99% and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck = 0; if not, plan a separate c6i.2xlarge change (needs stop/start)

#### 4.4 Confirm the queue-length alarm returns to OK
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-a-io2-queue-length --region us-east-1 --query 'MetricAlarms[0].[StateValue,StateUpdatedTimestamp]'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the queue-length alarm returns to OK

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the original 1,000 IOPS after the first change reaches…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original 1,000 IOPS after the first change reaches optimizing/completed
**Risks:** Reinstates the IOPS cap and higher write latency, Consumes another of the 4 daily modifications

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Make the higher io2 IOPS setting for vol-0123456789abcdef0 permanent in the infrastructure definition
**Description:** Wherever this volume (Name example-a-io2, Project example) is defined as code, set iops to the validated value (3,000 or higher) so a later deploy does not reset it. If the instance must grow, also update c6i.xlarge to c6i.2xlarge.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The template sets Iops for vol-0123456789abcdef0 to the validated target and a plan/diff shows no drift against the live volume.
- Summed throughput of all volumes on the instance stays within the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s.
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck stays at 0 and example-a-io2-queue-length stays OK under normal workload.

     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.

     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.

For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).

     131	## Critical Rules

     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App).      150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.

     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action, written as described in [Change proposals](#change-proposals).
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).
     13	
     14	## Limits table for performance verdicts
     15	
     16	Every performance verdict puts the numbers side by side in one table under Evidence, so the reader can see which limit binds without doing the arithmetic. Use the values measured in this session, with the time window.
     17	
     18	| Layer | Measured demand | Limit | Headroom | Binds? |
     19	|---|---|---|---|---|
     20	| Volume `<id>` IOPS | `<n>` IOPS | provisioned `<n>` IOPS | `<n>` IOPS | Yes or No |
     21	| Volume `<id>` throughput | `<n>` MiB/s | `<n>` MiB/s (provisioned for gp3, computed from IOPS for io1 and io2) | `<n>` MiB/s | Yes or No |
     22	| Each other attached volume, including the root volume | `<n>` IOPS, `<n>` MiB/s | its own limits | | |
     23	| Instance EBS baseline (sum of all attached volumes) | `<n>` IOPS, `<n>` MiB/s | `<n>` IOPS, `<n>` MB/s from `DescribeInstanceTypes` = `<n>` MiB/s | `<n>` IOPS, `<n>` MiB/s | Yes or No |

     25	Below the table, first give the exceeded checks from Step 2a of [troubleshoot-performance.md](troubleshoot-performance.md): for `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck`, `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck`, the number of minutes at 1 in the window, or "no datapoints".      26	
     27	- Show the tie-out arithmetic that links the numbers, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB average I/O size = 125 MiB/s, which is the provisioned throughput". Average I/O size = bytes / operations over the same period.

     30	
     31	## Binding-layer decision tree
     32	
     33	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.
     34	
     35	1. Is `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` or `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` at 1, is the summed IOPS or MiB/s of all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or are `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0?
     36	   - Yes: **Instance**. Say "the volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type". If a volume is also flat at its own limit, report both and fix the instance first, because volume changes cannot deliver above the instance ceiling.
     37	2. Is the instance healthy and one volume flat at its own provisioned limit on the dimension its type is judged by, or is its `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` or `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` at 1?
     38	   - Yes: **Volume**.
     39	3. Is a gp2, st1 or sc1 volume's `BurstBalance` draining or at 0?
     40	   - Yes: **Burst credits**.

     43	5. Are all layers below their limits, latency at the volume's normal level, and queue length low?
     44	   - Yes: **Not EBS**. Check CPU, memory, network and the application.

     57	An Indeterminate verdict is a short list of candidate causes, not a single sentence. The Binding layer stays Indeterminate, and the answer says so in those words: "Binding layer: Indeterminate".

     120	4. **For a volume modification:** the state sequence (`modifying`, `optimizing`, `completed`), the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window with each one completing before the next, and how many remain after this change from the AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` count (or say the count is unconfirmed and list it under Gaps).
     121	5. **Rollback,** as the exact reverse command and when it is possible (after the change completes for a volume, and it counts toward the 4; size cannot be reduced).
     122	6. **Cost direction,** with a link to the pricing page. Do not type a price.
     123	7. **The approval statement,** in plain words: "A typed approval in chat is not approval. This change runs only as a directed action that an operator approves on the approval card." If directed actions are not available in this Agent Space, say so and say that the customer can run the command above with their own credentials.
     124

     127	## Escalation (shared capability)
     128	
     129	Escalate to AWS Support when either is true:
     130	
     131	- Scope signals: an open AWS Health event for the volume, Availability Zone or Region; several resources failing the same way; `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a failing status check.
     132	- A bounded investigation cannot explain the symptom: all layers below limits, no running AWS FIS experiment, no recent change, and the symptom persists.
     133	
     134	Specific cases:
     135	
     136	- Attach or detach stuck: the attachment stays in `attaching` or `detaching` and does not progress. Diagnose (instance state, device name, whether the volume is still mounted, any forced detach already tried), then contact AWS Support.
     137	- Modification in `optimizing` with `Progress` not increasing across several reads, or still optimizing after 24 hours. Tell the user the Amazon EBS User Guide says some performance changes take more than 24 hours, so this is a check, not a fault finding. Escalate with the evidence.
     138	- Snapshot stuck in `pending` with no progress change over the same kind of window.
     139	
     140	Evidence pack to include:
     141	
     142	1. Account placeholder, Region, volume IDs, instance IDs, snapshot IDs as read from the APIs
     143	2. The time window (first ALARM time, symptom start)
     144	3. Metric evidence with units (IOPS, MiB/s, latency, queue length, `EBSIOBalance%`, `BurstBalance`)
     145	4. Volume status and AWS Health results
     146	5. The latest `DescribeVolumesModifications` record per volume, and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events if that optional lookup was available
     147	6. What was ruled out and how
     148	7. The Gaps list

     152	Each review finding has:
     153	
     154	| Field | Values |
     155	|---|---|
     156	| Severity | `High`, `Medium`, `Low`, or `Indeterminate` (the data could not be read) |
     157	| Evidence | The values and API that show it |
     158	| Fix | A specific change with parameters |
     159	| Mutating? | Yes or No. Yes means the fix is a proposal for a directed action |

The Summary table is required, not optional, and it comes before any per-area detail.
